en: Commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts (Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra-vṛtti), Fascicle Upper, composed by the Silla śramaṇa Yiji.
Now, the root of the virtue of the precepts is that from which the Way arises; it is that by which the lineage of awakening is established and perpetuated.
The True Dharma cuts off the long-flowing stream and enables one to reach the other shore;
it delivers all sentient beings.
There is nothing that does not proceed from this.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata was first at the Tree of Enlightenment,
he initially established the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa.
This is truly the foundation for attaining tranquility and liberation from the burdens of affliction,
and the root for cultivating causes and realizing the fruit;
since it is designated as "restraint" (vinaya), [it serves this purpose].
There is no evil that it does not sever;
it is also called filial piety and obedience.
There is no good that it does not accumulate.
When its main outline is grasped, the ten branches are inexhaustible;
when its general headings are summarized, the sixty-eight [subdivisions] leave nothing out.
Illuminating the path of awakening, it is like the sun and the moon.
The adornment of the Dharma-body is likened to a jeweled necklace;
yet the merit required for its establishment is difficult to manifest.
However, the words and meanings of this precept-sūtra are profound and obscure.
An explanation should be composed because [the text] is difficult to understand; therefore,
first I shall provide a brief topical outline to indicate its essential purport.
The dharma of precepts is immeasurable, yet its essentials are solely receiving and following.
Receiving is the root of karma, wherein the dharma is initially received and fully integrated into one's person;
following is the subsequent maintenance of the mind, wherein one manifests conditions for protection and restraint.
First, it is distinguished that there are two types of receiving [the precepts].
The first clarifies how one obtains the precepts through favorable conditions;
the latter reveals how one loses them due to adverse conditions.
There are four points of discernment:
first, discerning the vessel of the recipient;
second, discerning the virtue of the teacher.
Third, the method for the three types of receptivity;
fourth, questions and answers to dispel doubts.
First, regarding the examination of the vessel:
One must possess two conditions to be a fit vessel for receiving the precepts:
first, the wholesome karma that can evoke the precepts;
second, the absence of the unwholesome karma that obstructs the precepts.
There are generally two types of those who feel inspired by the excellence of the precepts:
first, those of the bodhisattva lineage;
second, those who have made the vow for enlightenment.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Because a person who abides in the absence of lineage lacks that lineage,
although they may give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and engage in its preparatory practices,"
They are certainly incapable of fulfilling unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
for even if they possess the capacity, they will not do so unless they generate the resolve and cultivate the preparatory applications.
One does not swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi;
conversely, one should know that when these conditions are absent, realization is swift.
It is by possessing both of these factors that one can truly evoke the precepts.
Therefore, regarding the inquiry into those two conditions within the context of receiving the Dharma,
some say that one obtains the induction of the precepts when three factors are complete.
First, there is a superior spiritual lineage;
second, there is a superior aspiration;
third, there is a superior mind of practice.
The first two are as before.
The third, superior practice, briefly consists of ten kinds.
First, being able to generate a profound resolve for unsurpassed bodhi.
Second, they are able for the duration of their lives to distance themselves from evil associates and draw near to virtuous associates.
Third, they are able for the duration of their lives to repent of transgressions, rejoice in merit, request [the turning of the wheel of Dharma],
and dedicate [their roots of goodness] toward the increase of the Buddha-way.
Fourth, they are able to provide offerings to the Triple Gem for as long as they live, according to their capacity.
Fifth, they are able to read, recite, copy, and explain the Vaipulya sutras for others for as long as they live.
Sixth, he is able to provide protection and relief according to his capacity for those who are solitary, impoverished, suffering, or have committed offenses against the king,
even generating a single thought of compassion. Seventh,
he is able to abandon indolence for the duration of his life and initiate diligence, earnestly seeking the path to Buddhahood.
Eighth, when afflictions arise regarding the five sensory objects,
he is able to investigate and subdue them.
Ninth, if a mind of weariness or retreat arises toward unsurpassed enlightenment...
When attachment arises toward minor dharmas,
he immediately eliminates it.
Tenth, he is able to relinquish all possessions without sparing even his own body or life.
These three are the three sustainments of a bodhisattva:
noble lineage is the sustainment of capability;
and the supreme vow is the sustainment of the application of practice.
Superior conduct is the support for great enlightenment;
the passage cited previously is precisely the proof for this.
Therefore, one obtains the realization of the precepts by means of these three factors.
When one is about to receive [the precepts],
it is necessary, as a matter of principle,
to pose questions and challenges; the original text does not include a third question.
Furthermore, because the three [types of lineage] are fully explained within the distinct categories of dharmas,
the "superior spiritual lineage" refers to that which is both innate and cultivated through practice by a bodhisattva.
The two types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) are explained at length in the treatise.
As for the bodhicitta,
it refers to the resolve to definitely realize the unsurpassed fruit.
One should give rise to the vow to certainly rescue all sentient beings,
and regarding these two matters, one should develop a firm resolve that cannot be diverted or overturned by any other conditions.
Furthermore, one observes that one's own nature is identical to that of a Buddha;
yet, due to the deficiency of internal and external causes and conditions,
one has undergone birth and death from beginningless time until the present body.
Never at any time have you generated the supreme aspiration;
drifting along with conditions, there is no day of liberation.
Now, if for even a single moment you generate a courageous mind, [you shall escape].
Though the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are long, the realization [of Buddhahood] must surely have its appointed time.
With sorrow preceding and joy following, with sweat flowing and tears falling in succession,
he disregarded his own body and life to make a resolute vow.
Birth and death are boundless;
I shall surely sever them.
Sentient beings are innumerable.
I shall certainly deliver them.
May my practice be immeasurable.
I shall surely cultivate it.
"The fruit of Buddhahood is inexhaustible;
I shall certainly realize it.
Such is called the characteristic of the arousal of the mind.
Those who obstruct the precepts do not exceed three obstructions:
first, the affliction obstruction;
second, the karma obstruction.
Third, the obstacle of retribution.
Regarding the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
What are the four secondary afflictions that contradict the specific nature of a bodhisattva of the lineage?
They are as follows: first, the heedless person, who, due to prior habitual practice of the various afflictions...
One whose nature is characterized by fierce and long-lasting afflictions is called the first type.
Furthermore, there is the deluded person.
The second is being dependent on evil friends due to a lack of skillful means.
Furthermore, it is being constrained and coerced by elders, husbands, kings, thieves, enemies, and the like.
Being unable to master one's own mind, one becomes deluded and distracted;
this is called the third [hindrance].
Furthermore, those who lack the necessities of life become preoccupied with their own bodies and lives.
This is called the fourth.
Since the treatise states that this constitutes a principle of obstruction to one's own dharmas,
it should likewise constitute an obstruction to the goodness of receiving the precepts.
However, the reason why these are not asked separately within the context of receiving the precepts is that they are not definitive;
they do not constitute a fixed impediment to receiving the precepts in the same way that the seven grave prohibitions (*saptāvaraṇa*) do.
There are two kinds of karmic obstructions:
first, the seven heinous offenses;
second, the ten grave transgressions.
The seven heinous offenses are:
first, shedding the blood of a Buddha;
second, killing one's father.
Third, killing one's mother;
fourth, killing one's preceptor;
fifth, killing one's ācārya.
Sixth, breaking the *saṃgha* by subverting the *karmavācanā* and turning back the wheel of the Dharma;
seventh, killing an *ārya*.
The specific characteristics of these seven will be made clear in the text itself.
The text states:
"If one possesses the seven obstructions, one cannot receive the precepts in this very body;
all other persons may receive the precepts."
Some say: "If one has committed the seven heinous offenses, one may not receive [the precepts] without repentance;
if one repents, one may receive them."
Therefore, the *Dharmarati-saṃgraha-sūtra* states:
"When Cāṇakya had committed the five heinous crimes and was being executed by the king,
he was struck with terror and immediately became a śramaṇa."
While practicing the ten wholesome deeds, sitting in meditation, and studying the Way in another country,
he wept day and night for thirty years;
yet because of the obstruction of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), his mind could not attain concentration.
Within the mountain cave, she constantly raised her voice in weeping:
"Alas! Alas! With what mind shall I depart from this suffering?"
On one occasion, as he was about to go out for alms,
he sighed with compassion, descended from his cave, and went toward the village; on the way,
he obtained a large begging bowl.
Within his alms bowl, he saw the *dhāraṇī* titled "The Joyful Abandonment of Suffering through the Dharma of Accumulation.
Having obtained this sūtra,
he immediately ceased begging for food and returned to his cave with great joy.
They burned incense, prostrated themselves, and sighed with tears of compassion and veneration.
By practicing and reciting this sutra within the cave for one year,
they finally succeeded in extinguishing their transgressions.
Because of karmic obstructions, one is unable to enter the mind.
At that time, one should immediately bathe and practice for seven days;
like a child first learning, one must be careful not to be negligent.
He practiced in this manner for seven days with such vigilance that there was no variation;
his heart was filled with grief and distress, not knowing what his intention should be,
so he contemplated the written characters of this dhāraṇī.
After several repetitions, his mind suddenly became settled.
At that time, he felt spontaneous joy,
like a person who finds gold weighing hundreds of thousands of catties in the earth, yet no one else knows of it.
His inner joy did not cease;
after practicing for several years,
he attained unimpeded power of flight.
One beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
thus, one knows that even the gravest offenses (*ānantarya-karma*) can be repented and extinguished.
Although this teaching exists, it does not yet constitute definitive proof.
This sutra speaks directly of the power of the scripture to extinguish transgressions,
but it does not state that one thereby receives the bodhisattva precepts; therefore,
one should examine the original source more carefully.

Regarding the "ten grave [offenses]," some say that since the first four among the ten are fundamental nature-offenses (prakṛti-sāvadya), their substance is identical to the seven heinous transgressions (ānantarya).
In this present life, both having such regret and not having it are all obstacles.
Regarding the other six grave offenses,
if one has no regret, they are not obstacles.
Lack of remorse constitutes an obstacle.
However, according to the scriptural text, those who have committed the ten grave offenses may receive the precepts provided they repent and attain the appropriate signs;
otherwise, they cannot.
This is a general statement; the intended meaning lies in the latter six.
Some say that the first four karmas are the most grave.
One must repent; upon seeing the signs, one may then receive [the precepts].
Without the signs, the precepts are not obtained.
The latter six karmas are light.
Although one may receive [the precepts] even without performing repentance,
the ten grave offenses must be repented;
this is a general statement, the meaning of which lies in the first four.
Some say: "If one currently commits the ten grave offenses and does not repent, all are obstacles;
if one repents, one may receive [the precepts] in their entirety."
The text contains no such distinction;
why then resort to such convoluted inquiry?
Such is the traditional explanation.
There is further a distinct meaning,
which shall be clarified in the text.
Regarding "obstructions of retribution" (vipākāvaraṇa):
Those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals who do not understand speech cannot comprehend one another due to the intensity of their suffering; therefore,
it is logically impossible for them to receive [the teachings].
Furthermore, among those in the human realm, those of the Northern Continent and other such classes are by nature dull and ignorant, failing to understand cause and effect;
their wills are weak and inferior, lacking resolute determination.
Such types as these also constitute obstacles to receiving [the teachings].
As for the question of why the hells and so forth are not mentioned separately among the obstructions:
their characteristics are so manifest that there is no risk of confusion;
thus, it is unnecessary to ask about them.
Regarding those who are stubborn and dull-witted, they are excluded from the section on vows;
furthermore, according to the *Mūla-karma-sūtra*,
beings in all six realms of existence may receive [the precepts].
Therefore, that sutra states:
"Sentient beings of the six realms may receive the precepts;
provided they understand the words, they obtain the precepts and shall not lose them."
One should know that there are light and heavy [degrees of retribution] in the hells.
Those who have committed heavy offenses do not obtain [liberation],
yet those with light offenses may still receive it.
Within the three realms, the realms of desire and form are beyond words;
as for the formless realm, it is not spoken of in terms of manifestation,
yet even honey is not excluded from it.
Furthermore, according to the case of a lay bodhisattva receiving the upāsaka precepts,
there are additional prohibitions and obstacles that must be inquired about and answered.
Therefore, the *Upasampadā-vidhi* states:
At that time, the bhikṣu should speak as follows:
"Do your parents, wife, children, slaves, and the ruler of the country permit you?"
If one says they consent,
one should further ask:
"Have you not incurred debts for the property of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha, nor for the property of others?"
If he says he does not owe anything,
one should further ask:
"Within your present body, do you perhaps have any illness of the internal or external body or mind?"
If one says "no," one should further ask:
"Have you not committed an unrighteous act toward a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī?"
Such matters as these are also obstacles to the precepts;
therefore, they must be excluded by means of questioning.
Regarding the virtues of the teacher:
One must possess four virtues to be qualified as a teacher for bestowing the Bodhisattva precepts.
First, one must be a fellow-practitioner of the Dharma (*sahadharma-bodhisattva*),
thereby distinguishing oneself from those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Second, they have already made the great vow,
thereby distinguishing them from those who have not yet resolved their minds;
third, they possess wisdom and power.
That is to say, being able to understand and retain both the words and their meanings;
and fourth, being able to transmit and elucidate the meaning expressed through speech—
meaning that one speaks with clarity and eloquence when teaching the Dharma to others, opening their minds and causing them to understand.
Furthermore, Master Kumārajīva said:
"One who possesses five virtues should serve as a teacher.
First, they must firmly uphold the pure precepts."
1. Having completed two years [of ordination] and ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*).
2. Being thoroughly proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka.
3. Masterfully penetrating the contemplations of dhyāna.
The *Pañcajñānagarbha* exhausts the profound mysteries.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Moreover, bodhisattvas do not seek to receive the pure bodhisattva precepts from anyone who is devoid of the wisdom of listening."
One who lacks pure faith should not receive [the precepts]; that is,
regarding such pure ethical discipline as has been received.
From the outset, lacking faith and understanding, they are unable to enter [the path]; they possess unwholesome thoughts,
and are characterized by stinginess and greed,
being corrupted by stinginess and greed.
One who has great desires and is not content should not be followed as a teacher.
Those who have violated the pure precepts;
those who lack reverence for the various points of training;
and those who are negligent and lax regarding the restraint of the ethical code.
One should not receive [the precepts] from one who possesses anger and resentment,
or who is largely intolerant.
One should not receive [teachings] from one who is unable to endure the transgressions of others,
nor from one who is indolent.
There are those who are indolent,
for the most part addicted to the pleasure of sleep by day and night, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of lying down;
they delight in associating with companions and take joy in idle chatter.
One should not receive [the precepts] from such a person.
As for one whose mind is distracted,
they are unable— even for as long as it takes to milk a cow— to practice by dwelling with a virtuous mind on a single object.
One should not receive [the precepts] from one who is dim-witted or of a foolish nature.
One who possesses an extremely inferior mind and slanders the Bodhisattva Sūtrapiṭaka and the Bodhisattva Mātṛkā should not be followed for instruction.
The meaning of this passage is as follows:
one who is far removed from lack of faith and the six hindrances,
and who is fully endowed with pure faith and the six perfections.
Only then is one fit to be a teacher.
Thus, for those who receive and bestow the Bodhisattva precepts,
it is not easy to possess the necessary capacity as a requisite.
It is extremely difficult to find one who possesses the requisite virtues to serve as a teacher.
If one succeeds in finding such a person where the capacity of the recipient and the capability of the teacher meet,
then both the receiver and the giver will act in accordance with the Dharma.
The lineage of awakening shall be greatly propagated and the tree of the Way shall flourish;
its time of fruition may indeed be foreseen.
Regarding the formal procedures for receiving the precepts, there are briefly six gates.
First, manifesting virtues to encourage acceptance;
second, distinguishing the superiority or inferiority of conditions;
third, the collective and individual aspects of the sevenfold assembly.
Fourth, the relative magnitude and sequence;
fifth, the explicit exposition of the method of receiving [the precepts];
sixth, the comparative evaluation that reveals its superiority.
Regarding the exhortation to receive [the precepts] for the sake of manifesting virtue,
the text states:
"When sentient beings receive the Buddha's precepts..."
Immediately entering the rank of all Buddhas, one becomes equal to the Great Awakening;
having already truly become a child of all Buddhas.
As the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Acts) says:
Entering the ocean of the Triple Gem has faith as its foundation;
dwelling in the family of the Buddha has the precepts as its foundation.

Whether male or female, those who have newly begun their practice as bodhisattvas and have first resolved to leave the household life, desiring to succeed to the rank of a bodhisattva— [should do so].
One should first receive the precepts of the True Dharma.
These precepts are the root of the treasury of merit for all practices.
It is the direct path toward the fruit of Buddhahood and the root of all practices.
This precept can eliminate all great evils, the seven views, and the six attachments;
it is the bright mirror of the True Dharma.
It further states:
"Once a Son of the Buddha has received the ten inexhaustible precepts,
the recipient transcends the four māras and overcomes the sufferings of the three realms."
From birth to birth, one does not lose this precept;
it constantly follows the practitioner until the attainment of Buddhahood.
If there were any sentient beings of the past, future, or present who did not receive these Bodhisattva precepts, [they would not attain liberation].
They cannot be called sentient beings with consciousness,
for they would be no different from animals;
nor can they be called humans.
Constantly separated from the ocean of the Triple Gem,
neither bodhisattva, nor male, nor female, nor ghost, nor human—
such are called animals.
This is called wrong view;
it is called the way of the heterodox;
it does not accord with human nature.
Therefore, one should know that the Bodhisattva precepts have a method for receiving them but no method for relinquishing them;
even if they are transgressed, they are not lost and persist until the end of the future limit.
Furthermore, a Dharma Master is able [to establish them] within all lands.
If this Dharma master converts a single person to leave the household life and receive the Bodhisattva precepts,
his merit surpasses that of one who constructs eighty-four thousand stupas;
how much more so if it be two, three, or even hundreds of thousands of persons!
The fruit of merit is immeasurable.
As for the teacher, husband,
wife, and the six types of close relatives may mutually serve as teachers and bestow instruction upon one another.
Those who receive the precepts enter the realm of all Buddhas and the ranks of Bodhisattvas,
transcending the suffering of birth and death for three kalpas;
therefore, one should receive them.
It is better to possess [the precepts] and yet transgress than to lack them and not transgress.
One who possesses transgressions is called a bodhisattva;
one who lacks them is called a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
Regarding the superiority or inferiority of conditions, the Sūtra states:
"There are three ways of receiving the precepts.
First, one receives the authentic, superior-grade precepts in the actual presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
Second, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
if there is within a thousand li a Bodhisattva who has previously received the precepts,
one should invite them to serve as a Dharma Master to instruct one in the precepts.
I shall first prostrate at his feet and speak thus:
"I request the Great Venerable One to be my teacher and grant me the precepts."
His disciples obtain the precepts of the True Dharma;
this is the middle grade of precepts.
Third, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
When there is no Dharma Master within a thousand li,
one should kneel on the ground with palms joined before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva and take the precepts by making this vow,
speaking as follows:
I, [Name], inform the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas of the great earth:
I am one who studies all the bodhisattva precepts;
these are the precepts of the lower grade.
The second and third [times] were also spoken in this way.
O Son of the Buddha, these three ways of receiving the precepts have been taught by past Buddhas and will be taught by future Buddhas.
The Buddhas of the present now teach it;
the Bodhisattvas of the past have already studied it;
the Bodhisattvas of the future shall study it.
The present bodhisattvas now study this true Dharma precept of all the Buddhas;
for if all Buddhas and all bodhisattvas were not to enter this gateway of the Dharma precepts, [they could not attain enlightenment].
It is impossible for one who has attained the fruit of the unsurpassed path to dwell on the stage of equality with empty space.
Regarding the seven classes of followers, both collectively and individually:
Among the three types of precepts, those that encompass wholesome conduct and those that sustain sentient beings are for the most part similar for both monastics and laity;
however, the precepts for restraining misconduct differ according to the specific protocols of the seven classes of practitioners.
Now, we shall distinguish their general and specific aspects based on the precepts for restraining misconduct.
There are two methods for receiving the vows of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*):
first, receiving them collectively with the other two;
second, receiving them individually with the other two.
The general reception of the ritual procedures is the same for all seven classes of followers without distinction,
because they all receive them by reciting the three sets of precepts collectively;
therefore, a single *karmavācanā* applies to all seven classes.
As for the various ways in which the secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are maintained, each differs;
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Dizhi) and the *Upāsakasaṃvarāṣṭaka* (Shouchufa) are precisely concerned with this.
If one receives them separately, the dharmas of the seven classes of followers (*saptasaṅgha*) differ.
If the two groups of the laity receive the five precepts,
regarding their specific characteristics,
it is further stated that there are six grave and twenty-eight light offenses.
It is exactly as described in the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*.
On the way, he fully received the dharma from the two assemblies according to the *jñapti-karman* rite,
following a group of ten or more monks.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Those who receive the worldly disciplinary precepts obtain them only after the fourfold formal motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
This refers precisely to this.
Regarding the three lower assemblies, each follows its own respective dharma, which is identical to that of the śrāvakas.
As for the distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles and their respective sequences,
there are two points therein.
First, small first and large later;
second, large first and small later.
If one first receives the small and later receives the large:
Regarding the previous Hīnayāna precepts, do they cease or do they remain? Furthermore,
as for [precepts] such as non-killing, which are identical to those of the Śrāvakas,
are these newly acquired, or are they simply the former precepts?
One interpretation states:
When the mind is redirected, the small becomes transformed into the great;
therefore, the previously held small precepts remain without being discarded.
However, it cannot be called the precepts of the Hīnayāna;
because the mind has been turned [toward enlightenment], they are not newly increased beyond the śrāvaka precepts.
If they were unique precepts (asādhāraṇa-śīla), they would be newly acquired at the time of reception.
The second [master] says:
"At the time of newly receiving [the precepts] by turning the mind,
although one does not abandon the former [precepts],..."
Furthermore, due to differences in the specific intention (*āśaya*), one further increases the abstinence from killing and so forth,
just as when receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*),
one additionally acquires the abstinence from killing and other precepts.
Regarding "the great first and the small later":
if one regresses from the Great [Vehicle] and enters the Small, one immediately loses the Great precepts;
if one does not regress from the Great but follows and studies the Small, one does not lose the prior Great [precepts].
Although one may receive the śrāvaka precepts,
they are not called a person of the Hīnayāna.
As for the correct method of receiving them:
According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
there are eight procedural rules.
First, requesting a teacher.
The text states:
"If bodhisattvas— whether they be householders or those who have gone forth— desire to diligently train in these three collections of precepts that constitute the bodhisattva's training..."
Having first generated the great aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

one should carefully seek out a bodhisattva of like dharma who has already made the great vow, who possesses wisdom and power, and who is able to transmit and elucidate the meaning through verbal expression.
Having first prostrated at the feet of such a superior Bodhisattva endowed with these and other virtues,
one should address him with this request:
I now wish to receive the bodhisattva pure precepts from you, O son of good family, or elder, or venerable one.
I pray that you will not decline my request for even a moment, however weary you may be.
"Out of compassion, please listen and grant [this].
Second, the power of seeking.
The text says:"
Having thus made this unerring request, he bared his right shoulder,

paid respectful homage to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and addressed the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages, attained great wisdom, and acquired great supernormal powers.
Being present before him, one should single-mindedly recollect all those merits and request the precepts three times.
The text says:
According to the power of their respective functional causes,
they give rise to a profound and pure mind or a modestly pure mind;
they show humility and reverence toward wise and powerful superior bodhisattvas.
Placing his kneecaps on the ground, or squatting or kneeling,
he makes this request before the image of the Buddha:
"I pray only that you, O Virtuous One," or "O Elder," or "O Son of Good Family."
Out of compassion, please bestow upon me the pure bodhisattva precepts.
Fourth, the cultivation of the pure mind.
As the text says:
Having made this request, he focused his mind on a single object and cultivated a pure heart, thinking:
"Before long, I shall attain an inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unsurpassed treasury of merit.
Having thus reflected upon these matters, he remained silent.
The fifth inquiry concerning the conditions:
At that time, a wise and powerful bodhisattva, with an undistracted mind,
whether sitting or standing, spoke thus to that bodhisattva who is capable of practicing right conduct.
"Listen, son of good family named [so-and-so],
or Dharma-brother, listen.
Are you a bodhisattva?"
He should answer, "Yes. [Question:
"Have you yet made the vow for bodhicitta?
He should answer, "I have already made it."
Sixth, the formal acceptance (*samādāna*).
From this point forward, one should say these words:
"O son of good family named [Name], you are my younger brother in the Dharma through the precepts."
