in terms of their legal substance, exclusively established by the Mahāyāna.
Regarding persons, it is upheld solely by Bodhisattvas.
As for the "Root of Precepts" (śīla-mūla),
this present Sūtra of Precepts serves as the foundation for the practice of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, this practice of ethical discipline is the root of bodhi.
As a sutra says:
"Ethical discipline is the root of this unsurpassed bodhi."
One should maintain the pure precepts with a single-minded focus.
Furthermore, this brief exposition serves as the basis for the extensive version.
Next, regarding the word-by-word commentary:
Since this sutra was excerpted [from a larger work], it does not contain these three parts;
nevertheless, within its text, it is not without a preface and so forth.
From the beginning up to the words "all are called the first purity" constitutes the introductory exposition.

The Buddha told the sons of the Buddhas: "From here until the forty-eight minor precepts, these have been recited as the formal exposition for Bodhisattvas of the three periods—past, present, and future.
The remainder is for the purpose of circulation."
The initial section of the introduction consists of two parts:
first, the verses which constitute the "Exhortation to Believe" introduction;
second, the prose that constitutes the "Formulation of the Precepts" introduction.
Regarding the arrangement of these two as the introduction,
the *Benye jing* (Sūtra on the Original Acts) states:
"Entering the ocean of the Three Jewels takes faith as its foundation."
Dwelling in the family of the Buddha takes the precepts as its foundation.
Since faith and the precepts constitute the foundation for entering and abiding [in the path], they are arranged here as the preliminary sequence.
Furthermore, because faith is the foundation for receiving the precepts, faith is set forth first.
Since the precepts are what this treatise elucidates, it establishes the sequence of the precepts.
Within the "Exhortation to Faith" (Kanshin-sho), there are eleven and a half lines,
which are divided into two sections.
The first five lines of the introductory verses set forth the origin and development of the Master who taught the doctrine;
the subsequent six and a half lines praise the Dharma of the precepts and exhort one to receive them.
Within the former section, there are further two parts.
The first two and a half lines set forth the beginning and end of the manifestation of the body;
the latter two and a half lines reveal the beginning and end of the teaching of the doctrine.
Within the section setting forth the beginning and end of the manifestation of the body:
The first two lines reveal the fundamental essence within the lotus pedestal;
the next two lines reveal the responsive body upon the flower;
and the subsequent verse reveals the transformational form beneath the tree.
The latter half-verse summarizes the preceding discussion from beginning to end.
Question: How should these three types of bodies be correlated with the [three] bodies?
Answer: There are various explanations, as follows.
Now I shall provide one explanation.
The term Vairocana encompasses the meanings of both the self-enjoyment body and the other-enjoyment body.
This is known to be so for the following reasons.
The first fascicle states:
"Throughout a hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I cultivated the mind-ground and attained the realization of Vairocana.
Thus, one should know that this refers to the universal self-enjoyment [body].
For the sake of the multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms brought by a thousand Śākyas, he preached the Dharma of the Mind-Ground;
thus, one should know that this also includes the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
This is the manifestation of his body appearing in response to those whose spiritual capacity has reached the stages (*bhūmi*).
The Śākyamuni atop the flower is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) within this Pure Land.
This is known to be so for the following reasons.
This is because those who take the lotus as their vessel do not possess the characteristics of a defiled land.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states:
"Regarding the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), each presides over a hundred *koṭi* of lands."
This is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) manifesting the eight phases [of enlightenment] within this defiled land;
it is precisely these ten billion Śākyamunis that have been described.
Therefore, one should know that the body manifested upon the flower is this very one.
This is not a transformation body manifested within an impure land.
Furthermore, this verse states regarding those who are newly trained:
"Vairocana recites this; I likewise recite it."
Therefore, we know that this is not in contrast to the defilements of the earth;
rather, it must be in contrast to the manifestations assumed by those Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (trīṇi kula-putrāṇām).
Next, as for the ten billion Śākyamunis:
This refers to the manifestation of his body for those ordinary beings,
followers of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment within the four continents of this defiled land.
Some interpret it as follows:
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that a Bodhisattva on the second stage enters a thousand worlds in a single thought-moment and is able to see a thousand Buddhas;
this is because ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the specific practice of the second stage.
Therefore, for the sake of Bodhisattvas of the second stage, he manifests the bodies of a thousand Buddhas.
The Bodhisattvas of the second stage directly face the original Vairocana Buddha of those thousand bodies;
these thousand Śākyamunis are transformation bodies manifested within a single moment of thought.
It may indeed be thus;
there is no contradiction in principle.
"I, now Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal"—as for "I, now Vairocana":
Whose words are these?
They are the words of one Śākyamuni among the thousand Śākyamunis,
who says "me" because he is referring to his own person.
"Time" refers neither to the past nor the future, but is present right now.
"Sitting squarely" means sitting upright.
As for the "lotus pedestal":
This refers to the place where the lotus seed is attached within the lotus flower.
Its circumference measures one thousand triple-thousandfold world systems;
this is the measure of the seat, not the measure of the land.
The Lotus Treasury World (Padmakośa-lokadhātu) described in the *Avataṃsaka* is precisely the world-system that it governs;
above it are twelve Buddha-lands and seven world-natures (lokadhātutva).
The nine directions are likewise so.
This is the place where Rocana constantly turns the wheel of Dharma.

Upon the thousand surrounding petals, a thousand Śākyamunis further appear. Regarding the phrase "upon the thousand surrounding petals, a thousand Śākyamunis further appear": it means that upon each of the thousand petals encircling the central lotus, there further manifests a thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas.
This refers to the lotus pedestal upon which Vairocana sits,
which is surrounded on all sides by a thousand-petaled flower;
each individual petal is equal in size to ten billion [worlds].
Upon these flowers appear a thousand Śākyamunis.

On each flower are ten billion lands, and in each land is a Śākyamuni, each sitting beneath a Bodhi tree and simultaneously attaining the Way of Buddhahood. Regarding "on each flower are ten billion lands, and in each land is a Śākyamuni": [this means that]...
This means that within each of the thousand petals, there are ten billion (*koṭi*) lands of the four continents;
"ten billion" here refers to the number *koṭi*.
One hundred *koṭis* of such lands constitute a trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
Ten hundreds make one thousand;
ten thousands make ten thousand;
one hundred thousand makes one lakṣa.
Ten lakṣas constitute one prayuta;
ten prayutas constitute one koṭi.
Three thousand great thousandfold world systems constitute ten billion.
One thousand [worlds] constitute a small chiliocosm;
one thousand small chiliocosms constitute a medium chiliocosm.
A medium chiliocosm is equivalent to one *lakṣa*.
A thousand of these "thousandfold worlds" constitutes a "great trichiliocosm.
A great trichiliocosm corresponds to one hundred *koṭis*.
However, according to the new translations, one *koṭi* corresponds to a *lakṣa*.
This refers to ten thousand being the number for a *koṭi*.
In older translations of the treatises, *koṭi* corresponds to *kūṭi*;
this refers to ten million being the number for a *koṭi*.
According to the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
there is one Śākyamuni in each trichiliocosm; it is only here,
within Jambudvīpa among these four continents, that he attained enlightenment upon the Vajrāsana with his actual physical body.
In other parts of the world, there is no Vajrāsana;
it is not a place for attaining enlightenment.
There, he merely dispatches transformation bodies to deliver those who are ready to be saved.
According to the Mahāyāna teachings,
within the trichiliocosm there are ten billion lands,
and in each of these ten billion lands there is a bodhi tree and a vajrāsana.
Each of the ten billion Śākyamunis acts as a presiding lord.
The Śākyamuni who transforms this land says,
"I am the original body."
All others are my emanations.
Śākyamunis in other lands all speak in this same way.
Thus, by examining the branches, one understands the root.
The ten billion [buddha-fields] all mutually serve as one another's basis.
Discussing the derivative from the fundamental,
they are all emanations of Śākyamuni.
"Thus, there are thousands of billions of Vairocana’s original bodies.
Regarding "thus, thousands of billions," this means one thousand times a hundred billion; hence it is called "thousands of billions.
It does not refer to a dual enumeration of both "thousand" and "hundred billion."
The lower [sections] of the thousand billion [worlds] are all explained in this same way.
"Vairocana, the original body" indicates his fundamental nature.
As the sutra in the first fascicle says:
I have practiced the Mind-Ground for a hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
taking this as the cause, I first abandoned the state of an ordinary person and attained Equal and Right Enlightenment, being named Vairocana.
It abides within the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury World-Ocean.
This terrace is surrounded by a thousand petals;
each petal is a world.
For the sake of the thousandfold world-system, I manifest as a thousand Śākyamunis;
occupying these thousand worlds, I further proceed to a single-leaf world,
wherein there are again ten billion Mount Sumerus.
Ten billion suns and moons;
ten billion sets of four continents;
ten billion Jambudvīpas in the south.
Ten billion Śākyamuni Bodhisattvas sat beneath ten billion bodhi trees,
each expounding the *bodhicitta-bhūmi* (the ground of the mind of enlightenment) that you have heard.
The remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine Śākyamunis each likewise manifested ten billion Śākyamunis;
it was exactly the same for all of them.
The Buddha upon the thousand-petaled lotus is my own emanation body (nirmāṇakāya).
The thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are emanations of these thousand Śākyamunis.
I am the original source, named Vairocana Buddha.

When each of the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis leads a multitude as numerous as motes of dust to come together to my abode to hear me recite the Buddha’s precepts, the Gate of Ambrosia shall open. At that time, the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis will return to their respective sites of enlightenment and sit beneath their Bodhi trees to recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of my original teacher. This is spoken within the exposition of the beginning and end of the teaching.
The first five phrases reveal the teaching of the primary body,
namely, the thousand Śākyamunis teaching the assembly brought by the ten billion Śākyamunis.
The subsequent five phrases demonstrate the teaching of the secondary bodies.
Thereupon, the ten billion Śākyamunis preached to the assembly of that time:
"The Gate of Ambrosia is opened" means that because the Dharma of Nirvāṇa remains forever through even a single meal, it is called ambrosia.
Because one enters through precepts, they are called "gates.
To say that one now speaks of them is to open [them].
"Returning to the original place of enlightenment" means:
Each of the ten billion lands is the realm of transformation for this particular manifestation;
therefore, it is called the "Original Site of Enlightenment.
As for the Precepts of the Original Teacher:
The Buddhas take the precepts as their primary teacher.
The precepts are like the bright sun and moon,
and they are also like jeweled necklaces.
The multitude of subtle-dust bodhisattvas thereby attain perfect enlightenment;
this is recited by Rocana.
I also recite it in this way.
You, newly initiated bodhisattvas,
should receive and uphold these precepts upon the crown of your head.
Having received and upheld these precepts,
transmit them to all bodhisattvas.
Listen attentively as I recite them correctly.
Within the Buddha-dharma,
the treasury of precepts, the Prātimokṣa,
is sincerely and faithfully believed by the great assembly.
"You shall become a Buddha;
I have already become a Buddha.
Always maintain such faith as this.
The chapter on the precepts is now complete.
All sentient beings who possess a mind should embrace the Buddha’s precepts.
When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts,
they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas;
having attained a rank equal to that of Great Enlightenment, they are already one with the Awakened.
Truly, you sons of the Buddhas,
the entire assembly listens with reverence;
listen now with a sincere heart as I recite the praise of the precepts for exhorting others to receive them.
The first line praises the virtue of his precepts;
the subsequent five and a half lines exhort [the reader] to believe and accept them.
Within the praise, the phrase "like the bright sun" refers to this.
The simile of the sun represents the precepts of restraint,
for they can destroy the darkness of evil just as sunlight does.
The simile of the bright moon represents the precepts of gathering and sustaining beings.
Because great compassion gathers sentient beings just as the moon loves them all;
and because it is like a necklace of pearls, which symbolizes the gathering of virtuous precepts,
adorning the Dharma-body like a precious gem.
Regarding the attainment of perfect enlightenment:
through the three types of ethical discipline, one achieves the three fruits of Buddhahood;
specifically, the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-śīla) brings about the Dharma-body of the quality of abandonment (prahāṇa-guṇa-dharmakāya).
The precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla*) accomplishes the wisdom-virtue *saṃbhogakāya*;
the precept of gathering sentient beings accomplishes the compassion-virtue *nirmāṇakāya*.
Regarding the exhortation to receive [the precepts], the first two verses and one line of the middle section provide the instruction on the precepts and exhort one to recite and uphold them.
The final three verses and one line exhort the acceptance and upholding of the precepts and conduct.
Within the first [of these], there are further two parts;
the first verse and two lines exhort the formal reception and maintenance [of the precepts].
The next three lines exhort one to listen attentively.
Within the section on ethical conduct (*śīla*), there are again two parts;
the first two verses consist of three lines that exhort one to embrace it with faith.
The latter two lines exhort one to listen with reverence.

"One who constantly practices such faith and is fully endowed with the precepts" means that when the mind constantly maintains the two aforementioned forms of faith, it becomes capable of serving as a fit vessel for receiving the teachings.
Therefore, it is said that "the category of precepts is already complete.
As for the statement that "all those with a mind should receive the Buddha's precepts," this refers to all sentient beings who possess the faith to attain Buddhahood.
All should receive and uphold the precepts of all Buddhas;
this constitutes entry into the rank of all Buddhas,
according to the *Sūtra on the Divination of Observations*.
There are four stages of Buddhahood.
The first is becoming a Buddha through the fulfillment of the Dharma of faith;
this refers to relying upon the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*).
First, they possess resolute faith that all phenomena are unborn and unceasing, pure and equal,
because there is nothing therein to be wished for or sought. Second,
through their understanding of the fulfillment of all phenomena, they become Buddhas.
This refers to relying on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
Therein, one deeply understands the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and knows that the activity of the Tathāgata is without creation or fabrication.
Because one does not give rise to dualistic conceptions regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the mind has no expectations.
Third, one becomes a Buddha by virtue of the fulfillment of the realization of the Dharma;
that is to say, based upon the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*),
one attains non-conceptual, quiescent knowledge of the Dharma and inconceivable, spontaneous activity.
Because they are free from the thought of seeking.
Fourth, they become Buddhas because all their meritorious practices are fulfilled;
that is to say, by relying upon the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva.
Because it can eliminate all obstacles and bring an end to the dreams of ignorance,
those who now receive the Bodhisattva precepts must possess complete faith; thus,
one who attains the first stage of faith and fulfills the rank of a Buddha is said to "enter the Buddha-rank."
Fearing that [the reader] might think [the author] has already attained Buddhahood, he states:
"In rank, I am equal to the Great Awakened One; I am truly a son of all Buddhas.
Thus concludes the Prologue for Encouraging Faith.

At that time, when Śākyamuni Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment, he first formulated the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa: the dharma of filial piety toward parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem; the dharma of filial piety toward the Ultimate Way, wherein "filiality" is named the precepts and is also called restraint. The Buddha then emitted immeasurable light from his mouth. At that moment, an assembly of hundreds of billions of beings—including various bodhisattvas, the eighteen Brahmās, the sons of the six heavens of desire, and sixteen great kings—joined their palms and listened with a sincere heart as the Buddha recited the Mahāyāna precepts of all Buddhas. Within the introduction to these formulated precepts, there are two parts.
First, the preface by the compiler;
second, the self-preface by the Buddha.
Within the preface by the compiler, there are three parts.
First, the introduction concerning the establishment of the precepts;
second, the introduction concerning the emission of light;
third, the introduction concerning the assembly of the multitude.
Regarding the initial establishment of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa within the section on the formulation of precepts:
while the Śrāvaka precepts were gradually established according to circumstances twelve years after [the Buddha's enlightenment],
it was not so for the Bodhisattvas.
It was first established at one time while [the Buddha] was under a tree.
The reason for this is that the faculties of the śrāvakas are inferior.
If regulations were established in advance for matters that had not yet occurred, one would be subject to ridicule and slander;
therefore, rules were gradually established only as circumstances for transgressions arose.
Bodhisattvas possess superior faculties and practice immediately upon hearing the teachings.
There is no weariness or censure;
it is established immediately upon the occurrence of the causal conditions for an offense, without waiting.
This is according to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
During the first seven days after attaining enlightenment, he either experienced the bliss of the Dharma himself or reflected upon causes and conditions;
therefore, he did not yet arise to preach.
Only after the second week did he begin to engage in verbal instruction.
What is here called the "first formulation" should refer to the middle of the second seven-day period.
From the section on filial obedience (*xiàosùn*) onwards, there is a brief explanation of the names and meanings of the formulated precepts.
Briefly, its name may be explained through two meanings.
*Prātimokṣa* translates here as "individual liberation precepts."
The Abhidharma-śāstra states:
Because one separately guards all forms of restraint for the sake of seeking liberation,
it is called the prātimokṣa-saṃvara (the restraint of individual liberation).
Because restraint enables one to swiftly emerge from the suffering of birth and death,
it specifically guards against [transgressions].
This precept is capable of attaining the fruit of liberation.
Therefore, it is named "Prātimokṣa" (Individual Liberation) by way of its result.
Furthermore, at the moment one attains the precepts, one is individually liberated from the bonds of the three types of action;
hence it is called "Prātimokṣa."
This Pratimokṣa precept, as received by Śrāvakas, possesses only the sense of restraint;
because it is able to prevent what is non-virtuous, it lacks the sense of filial piety and obedience,
for it does not seek to encompass wholesome qualities or to benefit others.
If the precepts of a Mahāsattva possess both meanings,
the first is the meaning of filial piety,
because they are able to encompass wholesome qualities and so forth.
Second is the meaning of restraint,
because it enables one to distance oneself from unwholesome dharmas.
Filial piety toward one's parents is so called because they have given birth to and nurtured this physical form in the world.
Those who are filial and obedient to their teachers and monks nourish the Dharma-body;
the Three Jewels are the supreme realm for entering the Path;
and the Dharma of the Ultimate Way is the root for attaining the fruit.
Briefly, four points are cited to clarify filial piety and obedience.
First, "the mouth lets go" clarifies the emission of light, manifesting as an auspicious omen prior to the proclamation of the Dharma of the Precepts.
Second, "at that time, the great assembly of hundreds of billions" clarifies the gathering of the multitude.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"I now recite the Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas every half-month;
you all, bodhisattvas who have resolved for enlightenment, should likewise recite them."
Even the bodhisattvas of the ten stages of setting forth (*prasthāna*), the ten stages of nurturing (*puṣṭi*), the ten adamantine stages (*vajra-bhūmi*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*) recite this.
For this reason, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth.
Since it has an object and is not without cause, the light is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black.
It is neither form nor mind, neither existent nor non-existent, and not a phenomenon of cause and effect.
It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the root of practicing the bodhisattva path.
This is the root of the great assembly of all Buddha-sons.
Therefore, the great assembly of all Buddha-sons should receive, uphold, read, recite, and skillfully study it.
Listen attentively, O Buddha-sons!
If one receives the Buddha’s precepts, this applies to kings, princes, ministers, and officials;

bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; the eighteen Brahmā deities and the six classes of desire-realm devas; commoners, eunuchs, male and female libertines, slaves, the eight classes of ghosts and spirits, *vajra* deities, animals, and even those who are transformed beings.
Those who merely understand the Dharma Master’s words and fully receive the precepts are all called the foremost pure ones. Within the Buddha’s own introduction, there are also three [categories].
First, the method for proclaiming and reciting the precepts;
second, the causal conditions for the radiance;
third, the exhortation to receive and uphold [the teachings], and so forth.
Regarding the initial instruction on recitation during the half-month:
although his fruition and virtue are perfected, he does not forget the causal expressions;
although he recites at all times as if for a beginner.
Therefore, it is called the "Recitation of the Half-Month.
Those Bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds refer to those at the stage of the Ten Faiths.
Those at the ten stages of setting forth refer to those at the stage of the Ten Understandings.
It is also called the Ten Abodes,
and it is also called the Stage of the Cultivated Lineage (*śikṣāgotra*). As for its ten names:
These refer to renunciation, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, aspiration, protection, joy, and the supreme mind.
Because these ten types of dharmas constitute the initial arousal of the mind and the entry into the Mahāyāna, they are called "setting out" (*prasthāna*).
The ten "nurturing" factors are the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).
They are also called the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*).
Their ten names are as follows:
This refers to the mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, concentration, and wisdom.
Because these ten practices have already become inherent nature and nurture the embryo of the noble ones (*āryagarbha*), they are called "nurturing."
The ten vajras refer to the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
They are also called the lineage of the path of cultivation (*mārga-gotra*).
Because their skillful means (*upāya-caryā*) cannot be dismembered or destroyed, they are termed "vajra."
These ten names are:
faith, resolve, dedication, penetration, perfection, rectitude, non-retrogression, the Great Vehicle, non-conceptual wisdom, and the indestructible mind.
The ten stages are also called the "Noble Lineage."
The ten names are:
the Ground of the Equality of Essential Nature and the Ground of Good Intelligence of Essential Nature.
The Ground of the Radiance of Essential Nature;
the Ground of the Blazing of Essential Nature;
the Ground of the Wisdom-Illumination of Essential Nature.
The Ground of the Flower-Light Essence-Nature;
the Ground of the Fulfillment of the Essence-Nature;
the Ground of the Buddha’s Lion’s Roar Essence-Nature.
The stage of the essence of the Avataṃsaka;
the stage of entering the Buddha’s sphere of activity.
The detailed exposition of its characteristics is as described in the preceding fascicle of the sutra.
Therefore, the light of the precepts explains the causes and conditions for the descent of the light of Śakra.
That there are conditions and not no cause means that externally there is the superior condition of time and the collective response of sentient beings to the Dharma.
Because there is within [the Buddha] the fundamental cause of the Tathāgata’s great compassion,
he is able to manifest auspicious omens to symbolize the Dharma he is about to preach.
Regarding "light upon light," it means that the radiance emitted possesses many layers.
That which is neither blue, yellow, red, white,
nor black is not the five colors because the derivative is identical to the fundamental.
That which is neither form nor mind is...
Because it is not an obstructive condition. "Neither existent nor non-existent" means that it is not existent for ordinary beings,
nor is it non-existent for those of the Two Vehicles.
That which is not a phenomenon of cause and effect is not a phenomenon of suffering or its origin.
The fundamental practice of all Buddhas is the root from which the attainment of fruition arises.
The "root of the bodhisattvas" refers to the foundation of the causes [of enlightenment].
The phrase "the root of the great assembly, the sons of the Buddhas" specifically singles out the members of the assembly present at that time.
Next is the exhortation to receive and uphold [the teachings].
"That which should be received" refers to receiving them from a teacher for the first time;
"that which should be upheld" refers to protecting and maintaining them after having received them.
"Those who should recite" refers to the recitation of the words and phrases;
"those who learn well" refers to learning the meaning and intent.
From "if one has received [it]" onwards is the detailed explanation of the meaning of receiving.
The remaining three [categories] are omitted for brevity,
as the first includes the subsequent ones.
"Kings and others" refers to the noble classes among the laity and so forth.
"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs" refers to those who have previously received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) as śrāvakas, and it also includes the three lower assemblies.
"The eighteen Brahmās" refers to the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
What are the eighteen?
One explanation says:
the three lower [realms] each have three, making nine.
The fourth [dhyāna] likewise has nine [levels]:
namely, the three beginning with Anabhraka, the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and the Asaṃjñin-sattvas.
Since it is admitted that the Asaṃjñin-sattvas possess minds at both the initial and final moments, [the same applies to the others].
It is possible for there to be those who resolve their minds to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
Since the sutras state that those descending from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens receive the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment,
we know that there are indeed those who resolve their minds to receive the precepts.
Some say that there are eighteen distinct Brahma heavens,
and that the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), including the Realm of Non-conception (asaṃjñika), are not included within their number.
As listed in the *Mūlakarma-sūtra* among the deities of the Form Realm (rūpāvacara),
namely: the Brahmā Heaven and the Brahmakāyika Heaven.
The Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (Brahmapurohita) and the Great Brahma Heaven (Mahābrahmā)— these four are the heavens of the first dhyāna. [Furthermore,
there are] the Water-Vehicle Heaven (Abhasvara) and the Heaven of Subtle Water (Parittābha).
The Heaven of Immeasurable Water and the Heaven of Water Sound—
these four constitute the heavens of the second dhyāna,
categorized according to the Pure Heavens (śuddhāvāsa).
The Heaven of Non-conception,
the Heaven of Universal Purity,
and the Heaven of Pure Radiance— these four constitute the heavens of the third dhyāna.
The Guardian of the Wondrous Heaven,
the Subtle and Wondrous Heaven,
and the Utmost Wondrous Heaven.
The Heaven of Meritorious Fruit,
the Heaven of Exalted Fruit,
and the Heaven of Great Tranquility— these six constitute the heavens of the fourth dhyāna.
The six heavens are the heavens of the desire realm.
As for the formless realm,
if one follows the teachings of the Exoteric School:
It is not mentioned because it does not pertain to the meaning of the dharma of non-sensation.
"Commoners" refers to those who hold no official rank.
"Eunuchs" refers to the five types of *paṇḍaka*.
"From animals up to transformation beings" refers to those among animals who possess the power of transformation;
provided they understand the words of the Dharma master, they may all receive and obtain the precepts.
Among those listed here, if one can comprehend the words of the Dharma Master and also give rise to the bodhicitta,
all such persons may receive the precepts.
Furthermore, the lay precepts are as explained above.
All who understand speech may receive it;
however, the case for monastic precepts is not like this.
Only among those in the human realm, whether male or female, provided they are free from prohibitions and obstacles, may they receive them.
Only then may one be permitted to receive [the precepts].
The meaning is the same as the method for receiving the Dharma upon leaving the household life as a śrāvaka.
Furthermore, all dharma-precepts should be received universally.
Since there is no distinction made in the text,
it should merely exclude those who possess the nature of a bhikṣu and so forth,
just as in the case of a paṇḍaka.
The permission to receive the five precepts has been granted;
however, one must strictly prohibit male lay followers (*upāsaka*).
The introduction is hereby concluded.

Regarding the section on the main body of the teaching (*śāstrakāya*) which encompasses the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddha, saying: "There are ten grave *pratimokṣa* precepts. If one has received the Bodhisattva precepts but does not recite these precepts, they are not a Bodhisattva and are not a seed of the Buddha. I, likewise, have recited them; all Bodhisattvas of the past have studied them, all Bodhisattvas of the future shall study them, and all Bodhisattvas of the present are now studying them. I have briefly explained the characteristics of the *pratimokṣa*; you should study them and respectfully uphold them with a reverent heart. Next, within the main exposition, the text is divided into two parts.
First, the identification of the grave precepts;
second, the elucidation of the light precepts.
Within the identification of the grave precepts, there are three parts.
First, the total enumeration of the names and teachings is presented so that they may be received and studied;
second, the specific characteristics of the types are described and admonitions are given to ensure their preservation and protection;
third, the gains and losses are summarized and concluded to exhort respectful upholding.
At the beginning and middle there are ten numbers;
"Prātimokṣa" is the name.
Regarding the phrase "one who does not recite it is not a bodhisattva," etc.:
This demonstrates that by means of these characteristics, one becomes established as the seed of a bodhisattva and a Buddha;
it shows that all bodhisattvas— those of the past, future, and present— are students of this very dharma of ethical discipline,
which is fixed and determined throughout the three periods of time.
As for the characteristics of the *mokṣa*,
not reciting [the precepts] is the mark of one who is not a bodhisattva;
this is precisely the characteristic of the precepts.
To study throughout the three periods of time is the very manifestation of the precepts.
This is explained separately within the section on the characteristics of the various types [of practitioners].
The ten grave precepts constitute the ten [categories].
Within each individual precept, the meaning of the text should be explained and analyzed by means of five points.
First: the intention behind the formulation and the explanation of the name.
Second, the completion of the offense through the presence of conditions;
third, the determination of the gravity of the karma;
fourth, the similarities and differences among the training rules.
Fifth, the explanation according to the text: Regarding the ten grave precepts, the Buddha said:

"O Sons of the Buddha, if one kills oneself, teaches others to kill, employs means to kill, praises killing, or rejoices upon seeing it done—even including killing by incantation; or if one kills through causes, conditions, methods, or karmic actions—up to and including not intentionally killing any living being—one must not do so. This Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of constant compassion, a mind of filial obedience, and employ skillful means to rescue and protect all sentient beings; yet if, on the contrary, they act according to their own indulgent will and take pleasure in killing living beings, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva."
1. The First Precept on Killing. Regarding the intent behind the formulation of this precept and its etymological explanation:
life is the root of the physical form and that which all living beings most highly value.
Among all sentient creatures, there are none who do not cherish it.
Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha cautioned King Ajātaśatru:
"Although there are distinctions between humans and animals, or between the noble and the humble,
there is no difference in the preciousness of life or the gravity of death."
Thus, since the Great Being prioritizes the cultivation of benevolence and compassion,
how could he permit himself to indulge his own whims or satisfy his desires by seizing what others hold dear?
Because this would specifically contravene compassionate conduct, it was prohibited first.
Furthermore, because the Śrāvakas prioritize liberation from bondage, they first prohibit sexual misconduct;
because Bodhisattvas prioritize compassionate salvation, they first forbid killing.
Moreover, since these ten grave precepts are observed by all seven groups of practitioners, the precept against killing is placed at the beginning.
Regarding the explanation of terms:
the continuity of the retributive form is conventionally designated as "birth.
To oppress and harm it through adverse conditions is termed "killing."
Regarding the completion of an offense through the presence of conditions:
the conditions for the completion of an offense consist of five general and five specific factors.
As for the five general conditions:
First, one has received the pure bodhisattva precepts.
Second, one abides in one’s own natural state and is not deranged or otherwise disturbed.
Third, one is not oppressed by severe suffering; otherwise, there is no offense.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"In all cases, there is no transgression" refers to when one's mind is excessively deranged by insanity.
If one is oppressed by intense painful sensations,
or if one has never previously received the pure discipline of the precepts (śīla-saṃvara),
these two conditions must be added to the meaning.
First, there is mindfulness:
that is to say, at the time of performing an action, if one remembers a previous undertaking, one commits an offense by following through with it;
if one does not remember, even if one performs the action, there is no offense.
Second, there is no opportunity to benefit sentient beings.
Since it is permitted to commit acts such as killing when there is an opportunity to benefit sentient beings,
the first three [unwholesome roots] and these two serve as common conditions for all five [paths of action].
Regarding the five distinct conditions,
the fifty-ninth [chapter] states:
"If one were to extensively establish the nature and distinctions of the ten paths of unwholesome action, they would further be categorized by five aspects."
What are the five? First, the thing;
second, the perception.
Third, the enjoyment of desire;
fourth, afflictions;
fifth, the culmination of skillful means.
Regarding "the basis" (*vastu*):
it refers to the specific, determinate objective bases for each individual path of action (*karmapatha*),
whether they belong to the category of sentient beings or to the category of non-sentient things.
The ten paths of unwholesome action proceed in accordance with what is appropriate.
There are four types of perception:
namely, first, perceiving something as not being that thing, as stated in the Vinaya.
1. Perceiving a human as a non-human.
2. Not perceiving that [object] as that [object], nor perceiving a human as a non-human.
3. Perceiving that [object] as that [object], and perceiving a human as a human.
In the fourth case, there is neither that object nor the perception thereof, neither a person nor the perception thereof;
for one who desires pleasure,
there may be either perverted perception or non-perverted perception.
The afflictions that delight in what is to be done are either greed, hatred, or delusion.
Whether it be greed and hatred, or greed and delusion, or hatred and delusion,
or the possession of all three— greed, hatred, and delusion—
the culmination of these skillful means is as follows:
One immediately applies the appropriate means for the action one intends to perform;
whether at that very moment or at a later time, the act reaches its completion.
Through these five characteristics, the taking of life is established.
This continues up to the paths of action of wrong view;
in each case, one should extensively establish their perfected nature as appropriate.
Such is the exposition regarding the tenfold distinctions in the treatise.
Now, following that perspective, I shall explain the conditions for this offense.
Regarding the "object" within killing,
it refers to sentient beings who are reckoned as such.
This consists of three grades.
The first is the superior grade,
referring to Buddhas and noble ones (āryas).
If one harms one's parents, teachers, or monastics, it constitutes a grave offense and is classified as a heinous crime (ānantarya).
Regarding those who have attained the three lower fruits [of the path],
one school of thought maintains that harming them does not constitute a heinous crime.
Because one kills while entering [the state of] nirvana according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
a bodhisattva who has reached certainty (*niyata*) is subject to the same category as killing.
One school of thought maintains that this constitutes a heinous crime (*ānantarya*).
Among the seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*), it is stated only that one kills a noble person (*ārya*);
it does not say "one who is beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
Therefore, killing a mother who is carrying a fetus [constitutes such an offense].
One view holds that it constitutes a transgression of the heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), because the offense against a bodhisattva is particularly grave.
Another view holds that it is merely a grave offense.
Because it is not the root of birth,
it is of medium intensity among the two;
that is to say, killing humans or devas constitutes only a grave offense.
The third is the inferior grade, which refers to the four lower realms.
One source states: [as follows].
If one harms [a sentient being], it constitutes only a minor offense,
for such a person is not a vessel for the Way;
as the text says, "all those who possess life."
This is merely citing a light case to illustrate a heavy one.
Even within the precepts of the Śrāvakas, it is stated that one should not take the life of even an ant;
how could this alone constitute a grave offense?
One interpretation states that it constitutes a grave offense,
because the text contains no qualification;
although in the Śrāvaka precepts it is initially stated in general terms.
Below, there is a distinction; herein it is not so,
for there has never been any distinction.
Thus, one knows that this is grave.
Regarding "perception" (saṃjñā),
the treatise says:
If one who intends to kill perceives a sentient being as a sentient being and gives rise to the desire to take that life,
this perception is called non-erroneous with respect to that sentient being.
However, there are three types of perception (*saṃjñā*).
First is non-perverted perception (*aviparīta-saṃjñā*),
which refers, for example, to a person forming the perception of a person.
The third phrase refers to various perceptions regarding those respective objects.
The fourth phrase refers to perceiving what is not a non-human as being a non-human;
these two constitute inverted perceptions.
That is to say, regarding a human, one perceives them as a non-human;
this is the first case: perceiving that [object] as not being that [object].
Furthermore, regarding a non-human, one perceives them as a human; this is the second case: not perceiving that [object] as being that [object].
Third, the three types of doubt-conceptions:
namely, doubting a human to be a non-human, and doubting a non-human to be a human.
Although this is not explicitly stated in the *Śāstra*, according to the Vinaya it should be understood that there are no inversions [in these cases].
If one perceives a human among two humans as committing a root offense,
there is no offense if it is a non-human perceived as a non-human.
If one regards a non-human or an animal [as a human], one also commits a root offense.

Now, since this concerns non-sentient objects, it is said that there is no offense; however, within the category of mistaken perception (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*), both [the first and second types] are fundamentally non-offenses.
Nevertheless, one should distinguish them:
in the case of the first person, who perceives a non-human as a human, because the fundamental perception is deluded, there is no offense.
If one changes one's perception, it is likewise an offense.

Even if one subsequently perceives a non-human as a human, although one does not commit the fundamental offense, one is nonetheless invariably guilty because of the commission of the preparatory act (*prayoga*).
Regarding those who seek sensual pleasure, the treatise states:
"Based on this perception, one forms such a thought as:
'I shall take life.'"
This is what is called killing.
The desire for this is the volition of killing; "desire" refers to the wish and so forth.
If one acts with a casual mind, one harms everything encountered;
if one acts with a casual mind, whatever objects are encountered all become the root [of the offense].
If one acts with a deliberate mind, when the mind and the object correspond, it immediately becomes the root.
If it is disproportionate or unsuccessful, it is considered light.
Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*), the treatise states:
"This harmer may be obscured by greed."
Some are afflicted by hatred;
some are afflicted by delusion;
and some are afflicted by both.
Alternatively, when a mind arises that is defiled by the three [poisons],
this is called affliction (*kleśa*).
Regarding the culmination of the preparatory means:
through desire and a defiled mind,
one initiates the preparatory means to harm sentient beings, whether by oneself or by inciting others.
If the victim dies immediately after being harmed, then at that very moment, by means of this very method,
it is said that one has accomplished the completion of the course of action (*karmapatha*).
If, however, the victim only dies at a later time, [the course of action is not completed until then].
Through these means, at the time of their death, they are said to have accomplished the path of action (karmapatha) to its ultimate conclusion.
Regarding the gravity of the offense incurred, there are three factors:
first, the distinction between the preliminary effort (prayoga) and the fundamental act (maula).
It is light because the preparatory stage lacks the necessary conditions and thus the action is not completed;
it is heavy because the fundamental stage possesses all conditions and the karma is fully manifested.
Second, within the fundamental stage itself, the gravity depends on the nature of the object.
This is because the karma is light or heavy according to the three grades of objects;
furthermore, within a single object,
it is light or heavy according to the lightness or heaviness of the mind, as the mind capable of giving rise to it possesses degrees of intensity.
The formation of karma is likewise so,
due to the distinction between defiled and non-defiled transgressions, as well as the difference in the state of mind (whether intentional or accidental).
The meaning of this can be understood.
Regarding the similarities and differences among the training rules (*śikṣāpada*):
these precepts are prescribed by both the Great and Small Vehicles, and they are likewise the same for both monastics and laypeople.
However, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are not entirely the same.
First, they differ regarding what is considered light or heavy:
for the Śrāvakas, only human beings are regarded as heavy.
In all other cases, the offenses are minor;
for a Mahāsattva, however, all three objects of the offense are grave.
Furthermore, there are differences regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited.
For śrāvakas, there is only prohibition and no opening;
for mahāsattvas, there is an opening whenever it is beneficial.
As the Bodhisattvabhūmi states:
If bodhisattvas, dwelling securely in the ethical discipline of the bodhisattva vow,
practice even minor forms of natural transgressions for the sake of benefiting others through skillful means.
By this cause and condition, one does not commit any transgression against the bodhisattva precepts and generates great merit.
This is as when a bodhisattva sees a robber who, out of greed for wealth, intends to kill many living beings.
Or, later, they may wish to harm a Great Virtuous One, a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha, or a Bodhisattva;
or they may wish to commit many acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya).
Having seen these things, they give rise to thoughts and reflect upon them.
"If I were to take the life of that evil person, I would fall into hell;
yet if I do not take his life, the karma of immediate retribution will be completed and I shall suffer great pain.
It is better that I kill him and fall into the hells."
He never causes them to undergo the suffering of the Avīci hell.
Thus does the bodhisattva reflect with such an intention;
having understood this matter regarding those sentient beings, whether with a virtuous mind or an indeterminate mind.
Out of concern for the future, one gives rise to profound shame and remorse;
with a heart of compassion, one takes that life.
By reason of these causes and conditions, there is no transgression of the bodhisattva precepts, and much merit is generated.
This is precisely the case with King Rūpāvatī, who killed five hundred brāhmaṇas; thus,
the methods for controlling the mind and controlling the body are not the same.
Regarding the text, there are three parts.
First is the designation of the person,
namely, the "Son of the Buddha."
Because those who have not received the bodhisattva precepts are not subject to these regulations,
they are treated like śrāvaka precepts, as in the case of a bhikṣu.
Second, the account of the offense.
If one commits these three offenses through one's own actions,
they constitute a pārājika offense for a bodhisattva.
In the account of the transgressions, there are again three parts:
first, citing what should not be done because it is prohibited;
second, from "A Bodhisattva" onwards, citing what should be taught and constantly practiced.
Third, regarding the mind’s own indulgence, whether it subsides or rises, it should not constitute an offense.
Within the first "should-not," there are again three parts;
the first six phrases clarify the nature of the offense.
The next four lines distinguish the completion of the offense;
the subsequent passage, "even unto all living beings," was judged by the ancients as citing a light case to illustrate a grave one.
Now, this refers to the boundaries of the offenses for the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding the matters of offense, the first two are easy to understand.
As for "attempting to kill" (*upakrama-māraṇa*):
For example, as with providing a weapon or medicine,
one praises the killer, thinking,
"By my praise, the person before me shall die."
Regarding those who witness and rejoice:
this refers to those who rejoice at the death of another,
up to and including those who kill by means of incantations.
This refers to spells such as the vīdara;
by reciting these spells, the person before one meets death.
There are many varieties of such acts of killing.
Because the remainder is abbreviated and only this is taken up, it says "up to and including" (*yāvat*).
For example, causing an abortion, placing [a fetus] in the womb, sending a messenger, sending a secondary messenger, and so forth;
such instances are not limited to one.
Regarding the commission of an offense:
as for the act of killing,
it constitutes the act of killing through any one of the three types of action (karma).
The method of killing refers to the means of killing, such as striking with a blade or shooting with an arrow.
The cause of killing is...
The "causative origination" refers to the mind;
the "conditions for killing" refer to the object, the perception, the intention, the affliction, and the preparatory effort.
As explained above,
that which is appropriate to practice is easy to understand;
now, returning to the discussion of what is inappropriate:
One who acts with a self-indulgent mind disregards and shows no hesitation toward what the Buddha has prescribed;
they act according to their own foolish impulses, following whatever conditions arise.
One who kills for the sake of gratification has no delusion within and no external compulsion.
To commit the act of killing with a clear and deliberate mind constitutes the offense of a *pārājika*.
This term means "falling into an undesirable state."
It is also called a "defeat" (pārājika).
One who has left the household life and received the precepts does so fundamentally to subdue Māra;
yet, by violating the precepts, one falls into an inferior state.
Therefore, it is said that one falls into an inferior state.
Because the other is superior and I am defeated, it is called a "defeat" (*parājika*).

If a disciple of the Buddha steals for himself, teaches others to steal, employs the means of stealing, praises stealing, or rejoices upon seeing it committed—even including stealing by incantation, through the causes of stealing, the conditions of stealing, the methods of stealing, or the karmic actions of stealing—and even including the property of ghosts and spirits, or goods belonging to owners or thieves, not even a single needle or blade of grass may be stolen intentionally. Yet, while a Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of Buddha-nature, filial piety, compassion, and kindness, constantly assisting all people to produce merit and happiness, if instead he steals another's wealth and goods, this is a *pārājika* offense for the Bodhisattva.
2. The Second Precept on Stealing: Regarding the intention behind the formulation of this precept and the explanation of its name—wealth constitutes one's external life;
as it is that upon which one depends for sustenance, there is nothing that people do not cherish and protect when it comes to their own selves.
A Mahāsattva, in his compassionate resolve, ought to assist others in generating merit and happiness;
yet, by instead encroaching upon and damaging the property of others to enrich himself and increase his greed,
he violates the path of conduct to a profound degree.
Therefore, it is next defined as "stealing.
"Stealing" (*steya*) is another name for taking what is not given;
the term "theft" (*steya*) is derived from this.
The term "kalpa" (劫) refers to manifest seizure;
theft applies to both types.
Regarding the full set of conditions for an offense:
Regarding the matter of taking what is not given, the *Śāstra* states:
it refers to property belonging to another.
According to some interpretations based on the Vinaya, one commits a grave offense only when taking human property worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more.
One says: "It is not so.
The text states that even for spirits and ghosts, there is property above them; one must not steal even a single needle or a blade of grass.
Therefore, we know this is distinct from the Śrāvakas."
"Perception" refers to perceiving another's property as one's own.
The four permutations regarding the inverted and non-inverted [perceptions] should be understood by analogy with the case of killing.
"Desire for pleasure" refers to the desire for theft.
"Afflictions" refers to those [afflictions] among the three types, whether occurring individually or collectively.
"The culmination of the preparatory effort" refers to...
That is to say, when one employs skillful means to move [the object] away from its original location,
the gravity of the offense incurred should be understood by analogy with the precept on killing.
Regarding the similarities and differences among the training rules (śikṣāpada), they should likewise be understood by analogy with the precept on killing.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Furthermore, it is as when a bodhisattva sees a superior official or a high-ranking minister who is extremely violent and cruel toward sentient beings,
lacking any compassion and exclusively engaging in oppression and affliction."
Having seen this, the bodhisattva reflects upon that evil;
giving rise to a mind of compassion and the aspiration for their benefit and happiness, he—
according to his capacity— dismisses or deposes them from positions of superior rank and the like.
By reason of these causes and conditions, one does not commit any transgression against the bodhisattva precepts and generates much merit.
Furthermore, it is as when a bodhisattva sees a robber or thief seizing the property of others or the property of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the property of a stūpa,
having taken much of it and claimed it as his own, he uses it according to his pleasure.
When a bodhisattva sees this, he gives rise to a heart of compassion.
One should give rise to the intention to bring benefit and happiness to those sentient beings;
one should, according to one's ability, forcibly seize their property so that they do not enjoy it,
for by means of such wealth, they will experience long nights of meaninglessness and disadvantage.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, whatever wealth and treasures were seized shall be restored: those belonging to the Saṅgha shall be returned to the Saṅgha;
those belonging to a stūpa shall be returned to the stūpa;
and those belonging to sentient beings shall be returned to sentient beings.
Furthermore, seeing monastery superintendents or park keepers take property belonging to the Saṃgha or to a stūpa and claim it as their own,
using it according to their whims, the Bodhisattva,
having observed this, reflects upon their misconduct and gives rise to a mind of compassion.
Do not allow yourself to undergo long nights of meaninglessness and disadvantage due to the karma of such improper enjoyment;
to the best of your ability, you should abandon what you preside over.
In this way, although the bodhisattva takes what is not given, there is no transgression and much merit is generated.
Regarding the text, as before, there are again three parts.
Within the section describing the transgressions, there are first four points that distinguish matters which should not be transgressed.
The fourth [offense], stealing through incantations, constitutes four clauses of an offense,
which are listed later.
Regarding the preparatory act of stealing, as the Vinaya states:
The bhikṣu who accepts the offering says to the donor:
"I accept your offering;
I am one such as an arhat. This is what is meant.
If one obtains such offerings, the offense involves two matters:
namely, lying and theft. As for "stealing by incantation": [it refers to obtaining through the power of spells].
Reciting mantras causes things to come of their own accord.
There is no "praising and rejoicing," because one's own karma is accomplished without depending on praising and rejoicing.
Regarding "spirits and deities who have ownership over objects":
this refers to objects within a shrine where either the deity or spirit itself is the owner,
or another being acts as the guardian and owner.
"Property of robbers" refers to goods confiscated by the authorities from robbers. Alternatively,
"property of robbers" may also refer to...
Although these were originally my possessions,
if they are seized through robbery, they become the property of the thief;
for there is no fixed ownership of objects, as whoever takes them becomes their master.

If a Buddha’s disciple engages in sexual misconduct themselves, teaches others to engage in sexual misconduct, or even intentionally commits sexual acts with any woman—whether through the causes of lust, the conditions of lust, the methods of lust, or the karma of lust—even with female animals, female devas, female ghosts, or female spirits; or if they engage in sexual intercourse through improper orifices—and yet this Bodhisattva, instead of generating a heart of filial obedience to save and deliver all sentient beings and bestowing the pure Dharma upon them, on the contrary gives rise to lust for all people, making no distinction between animals, nor even their own mother, daughter, sister, or other members of the six kinds of kin, acting without a heart of compassion—this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva.
3. The Third Precept on Sexual Misconduct. The division of the text for this precept is as before.
Regarding the intent of the prohibition and the explanation of its name, the Sūtra says:
If one does not sever lust, it will still obstruct the attainment of the Brahma-heaven,
let alone the realization of Bodhi.
That sentient beings remain bound by the bridle of birth and death and cannot escape is truly due to this.
Therefore, it is regulated and prohibited.
Excessive lust for sensual forms is called "lust" (*kāma*) and is also termed "non-celibacy" (*abrahmacarya*).
Although all precepts are non-celibate in nature, [this term specifically refers to sexual misconduct].
Because the fault of this defilement is particularly grave, it is singled out for mention.
Regarding the "factors" within the conditions:
all three objects are grave.
Furthermore, according to the Vinaya, only the three apertures of women and two locations of men constitute grave objects;
other locations are not grave.
If one follows the scriptural text:
Furthermore, sexual intercourse via improper orifices is likewise forbidden.
Thus, we know that for a Bodhisattva, even such acts are considered grave offenses.
Moreover, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Regarding the objective basis of the unwholesome path of action consisting of sexual misconduct:
it refers to that which a woman ought not to engage in;
or, even if she ought to engage in it, [engaging in it in an improper manner].
It is neither a constituent nor a locus;
it is neither a time nor a measure.
If it were so, it would be unreasonable.
All males and those who are neither male nor female,
whether they are [the mother] herself or those protected by the mother and so forth.
It is called "that which should not be practiced.
All parts other than the birth canal are termed "non-members" (*ananga*).
When [semen] flows out from these [non-members], it is impure.
When the fetus is fully developed;
when drinking the child's milk;
and when observing the fast and precepts.
Or when one is ill; that is,
when any illness makes it unsuitable to practice sensual desire—
this is called "inopportune time."
Whether at a gathering place of one's gurus,
within a sacred temple,
or before a great assembly.
Alternatively, hard ground that is uneven with highs and lows, causing instability—
such locations are called "inappropriate places" (asthāna).
To act beyond measure is called "improper measure" (amātra).
It is called "unreasonable" because it does not conform to worldly etiquette;
whether one acts on one's own desire or acts as a matchmaker for another.
Both of these are subsumed under sexual misconduct.
